one_liner: Meta's Rust rewrite of the Buck build system; up to 2x faster than Buck1 in Meta's internal monorepo usage.
what_it_does: Buck2 is a multi-language, hermetic build system and successor to Buck1, targeting ultra-large monorepos (C/C++, Rust, Python, Java, OCaml, and more via user-defined rules). It is not drop-in for Make/CMake/Cargo: projects are described in Starlark BUCK files plus a `.buckconfig`, and the build logic itself (even C/C++ support) is implemented as a Starlark 'prelude' rather than built into the core.
how_it_is_fast: Core build graph runs on `dice`, Meta's own incremental computation engine, so only invalidated nodes recompute on a change. Remote Execution support (Bazel's REAPI, works with BuildBarn/BuildBuddy/EngFlow/NativeLink) enables distributed/cached builds and, when used, hermeticity: all rule inputs must be declared or the build fails. A persistent background daemon (buckd) plus filesystem watching avoids repeated startup/scan cost on ultra-large repos. Build files and rules are parsed/evaluated with `starlark-rust`, Meta's own fast Starlark interpreter.
when_to_use: Large, multi-language monorepos already paying the cost of Make/Bazel-style top-down builds and needing better incremental-rebuild accuracy
Teams that can invest in Remote Execution infrastructure to get real hermetic, cacheable builds
Projects wanting a single build/test/query tool across languages with cross-language dependencies (e.g. Rust crate <- OCaml <- Python)
Teams willing to write/port BUCK/Starlark rule definitions instead of reusing existing CMake/Make/Cargo build files
Users comfortable tracking a fast-moving HEAD with no stable release tag
when_not_to_use: Small or single-language projects where Make/CMake/Cargo already work fine — migration cost isn't justified
Teams wanting hermetic guarantees without standing up Remote Execution: local-only build steps are not sandboxed/hermetic (README footnote)
Projects needing precompiled-header support: open issue #368 says PCH 'don't seem to be working'
Workloads sensitive to daemon startup latency: open issue #507 notes 'daemon startup is a bit slow'
Anyone needing a stable, versioned release: no stable release tag exists, Meta itself tracks HEAD

integration.dependencies: none (self-contained Rust workspace; Remote Execution backend optional and external, e.g. BuildBarn/BuildBuddy/EngFlow/NativeLink)
integration.min_toolchain: prebuilt binaries via GitHub releases or dotslash; building from source uses a pinned Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml: nightly-2026-07-05)
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (CI has setup_linux_env/setup_macos_env/setup_windows_env and a Cross.toml)
integration.thread_safety: not documented (daemon architecture is designed for concurrent builds; no explicit thread-safety contract found in README/source skim)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: replaces Buck1 with much better incremental-dependency accuracy per README, but requires BUCK/Starlark build files, not a drop-in for CMake/Make/Cargo project files

gotchas: Local-only build steps are NOT sandboxed/hermetic; only Remote-Execution-backed builds get full hermeticity (README footnote)
Open issue #340: buck2 recompiles *all* source files when a link-only dependency changes
No stable release tag; Meta itself runs latest HEAD, so 'rough edges' are expected for outside users (README warning)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Buck2 over Mill/tup/xmake when you need true multi-language monorepo builds with Remote-Execution-backed hermeticity and are willing to adopt Starlark BUCK files; its 2x number is Meta-internal Buck1-vs-Buck2 only (evidence tier C, no workload/hardware given), so it is not a verified head-to-head against Make/CMake/Ninja/Bazel/Cargo the way tup's or Mill's numbers are.
verified_claims_summary: The only first-party number is the README's 'up to 2x faster than Buck1 in practice,' sourced from Meta's internal production usage comparing Buck2 to Buck1 across Meta's monorepo. No specific workload, project, methodology, compiler/stdlib, or hardware is given, and the README itself says comparisons against Bazel-class systems 'have yet to be performed.'
status_note: Actively maintained (commits as of 2026-09-24, 4.4k stars, used in production at Meta), but usability is 'copyable' rather than a stable package: no stable release tag, dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed.
